items.text:
❄️ Pluto may still have liquid moving across its surface.

A new analysis of NASA’s New Horizons images has found evidence that liquid nitrogen may be rising through cracks in Sputnik Planitia, the giant heart-shaped glacier on Pluto.

This is not liquid water.

Sputnik Planitia is made largely of frozen nitrogen, and Pluto is so cold that nitrogen behaves there in ways water does on Earth.

The clue comes from dark, narrow and diffuse features along the northern edge of the glacier.

They resemble places on Earth’s ice sheets where liquid briefly wets the surface and darkens the snow or ice.

But on Pluto, nitrogen rain is physically impossible under its current atmospheric and thermal conditions.

That leaves a stranger possibility.

Computer models suggest that nitrogen ice at the base of Pluto’s kilometer-deep glacier could melt under stress, forming liquid nitrogen.

That liquid could then rise through small conduits, reach the surface and remain liquid long enough to flow downhill before freezing again.

The surface of Sputnik Planitia is probably less than a million years old, so these features may be geologically recent.

Pluto was supposed to be a frozen dead world.

Instead, it may still be leaking liquid from beneath its icy heart.

📄 RESEARCH PAPER
📌 Stern et al., “Evidence for Possible N₂ Basal Flow beneath Pluto’s Northern Sputnik Planitia”, The Planetary Science Journal (2026)

WEDNESDAY SEVERE THREAT: An active Wednesday awaits as WNY deals with multiple rounds of thunderstorms. Here's what you need to know-

ROUND 1: Scattered thunderstorms will develop Wednesday morning across WNY, interacting with a surface boundary. A few of these could be strong to marginally severe with strong wind gusts and hail possible.

EARY-SEASON WINDS FOR PNW🌬️⚠️🌲a strong early-season storm will bring widespread gusty winds to the Pacific Northwest on Wednesday, with some areas potentially seeing enough wind for downed tree limbs and power outages. One concern is that trees across much of the region are still fully leafed out, allowing them to catch more wind than they would during a typical fall or winter storm. After a long, dry summer, stressed trees and branches may also be more vulnerable, so expect scattered downed limbs and localized power outages, especially along the Washington and Oregon coasts. Secure loose outdoor objects and be prepared for brief power disruptions. Winds peak during the day Wednesday before gradually easing Wednesday night into Thursday.

Across Western Washington, gusts of 35-40 mph are expected along the coast, San Juan Islands and Whidbey Island, where a Wind Advisory is in effect. Western Whatcom and Skagit counties and the Port Townsend area could also see stronger gusts. Elsewhere across western Washington, gusts of 20-35 mph are expected.

Down into western Oregon, winds will become considerably stronger near the coast, with gusts along beaches and headlands potentially reaching 55-60 mph. Inland areas could gust around 30 mph, while the Columbia River Gorge and Hood River Valley could approach 40 mph.

Farther inland, the Inland Northwest will see south to southwest winds will gust 20-40 mph Wednesday, with some of the strongest winds across central Washington and the Columbia Basin. Blowing dust could reduce visibility in the drier areas🌬️⚠️🌲

items.text:
The night sky of September is magical 💫👇🏻

♀️ Sep 1: Venus Kisses Spica
Brilliant Venus slides right past Spica, the blue-white heart of Virgo. The dazzling planet and the star form a striking close pair in the fading evening twilight.
📍 Visibility: Low in the west-southwest, about 45 minutes after sunset. Binoculars help; far better placed from the Southern Hemisphere, where the evening sky stands steeper.

🌠 Sep 1–2: Aurigid Meteor Shower
A minor but intriguing shower peaks in the small hours, shed by comet Kiess on its ~2,000-year orbit. The Aurigids are sparse but famous for the occasional brilliant fireball.
📍 Visibility: Best from the Northern Hemisphere in the hours before dawn; the radiant sits in Auriga, rising in the northeast. A bright waning gibbous Moon washes out all but the brightest this year (~6/hour at best).

🌙 Sep 6–7: Moon Meets Mars
The waning crescent Moon glides up to reddish Mars in Gemini, close to the bright twin stars Castor and Pollux — a delicate pre-dawn grouping.
📍 Visibility: Eastern sky before sunrise, both hemispheres. Mars is faint this month, so let the crescent Moon guide your eye to it.

🌒 Sep 14: Moon Occults Venus
The thin crescent Moon passes directly in front of Venus, briefly hiding the brightest planet behind its edge — a rare occultation.
📍 Visibility: The true occultation is visible from parts of Asia (including Malaysia) and, in daylight, Europe; elsewhere it's a close Moon–Venus pairing low in the west after sunset. A tough catch, with Venus sitting low in bright twilight.

🍂 Sep 23: Autumn Equinox
Day and night fall into near-perfect balance as the Sun crosses the celestial equator. Autumn begins in the Northern Hemisphere; spring stirs in the Southern.
📍 Visibility: Worldwide. The equinox arrives at 00:05 UTC on Sep 23 (the evening of the 22nd in the Americas).

🌕 Sep 26: Harvest Moon
The full Moon closest to the equinox rises golden on the horizon, with ringed Saturn glowing close by. For several nights running it climbs just after sunset — the hallmark of the Harvest Moon.
📍 Visibility: Worldwide. Rises around sunset; look east as darkness falls, with Saturn (near opposition) as a bonus alongside.

This photo is a microcosm of what our lives looked like over the last few years before Mom passed.

As many of you know, her health was not great so she spent a lot of time in and out of hospitals, rehab facilities and doctors’ offices. One of her longer stays away from home was at Brightwater, where she went for rehab after surgery to repair a broken tibia.

We visited her every single day for several months. There were times when it was mentally and physically exhausting, but Mom thrived when we were there. She was always so happy to see us, and no matter how tired we might have been, seeing her smile had a way of reinvigorating us.

Looking back now, I realize just how precious those days were.

There were so many great conversations, so much laughter and a lot of reminiscing about when we were kids, and how Mom somehow managed to put up with all four of us. At the time, they were simply visits. Today, they’re memories I wouldn’t trade for anything.

This photo gives a whole new meaning to simply sitting on the porch and relaxing. Whenever we could, we’d get Mom out of her room and into the fresh air. Nothing fancy. Just sitting together, talking and enjoying each other’s company.

I guess all of this is to say that some of life’s most meaningful moments don’t happen in the places or circumstances we would choose. Even in places that are far from ideal or normal, wonderful and lasting memories can be made.

Sometimes you don’t realize just how special those ordinary moments are until you’d give anything to have one more of them.
❤️❤️

🍁HELLO, FALL!🍁

Well, meteorological fall, that is! It officially begins today. Astronomical fall, on the other hand, won’t kick in until September 22nd. So why the difference?

Astronomical seasons are tied to Earth’s position relative to the sun, while meteorological seasons follow the annual temperature cycle. In weather terms, winter is the three coldest months (Dec–Feb), summer the three hottest (Jun–Aug), with spring (Mar–May) and fall (Sep–Nov) bridging the gap.

And honestly? This is my favorite time of year. After sweating through a hot, sticky summer, I am more than ready for some crisp, dry, refreshing air.

QUICK UPDATE: I'm continuing to monitor the threat for severe weather Tuesday into Wednesday across WNY. Good news/bad news with some of the new data tonight. I think the threat for frisky thunderstorms late Tuesday has decreased. Woohoo, that's good news. Now the bad. 

Tonight's data is still pointing at a more robust threat developing later Wednesday within an environment defined by ample instability, wind shear & upper level support. It would not surprise me to see the Storm Prediction Center upgrade the region from a level 2/5 risk (for Wednesday) to a higher category in a future update. 

The map below plots STP (Significant Tornado Parameter) values for Wednesday evening. STP attempts to define the overall potential of tornadoes. Anything above 1 is worth paying attention to. To be clear, this does NOT mean we're talking about a tornado outbreak. Heck, it's certainly possible there are no tornadoes in WNY at all. We have many days with elevated STP values and nothing happens. What it does highlight is an atmosphere that appears primed for all modes of severe weather. Damaging wind, hail and perhaps a few tornadoes. 

This is likely to be a highly changeable forecast over the next 48 hours. We'll keep fine-tuning with hopes things start settling down. For now, consider this an early heads up we might need to be weather-aware later Wednesday. Stay tuned.

☄️ A quiet meteor shower with a wild streak peaks tonight, capable of surprising us with sudden bursts of fireballs.

The Aurigids reach their peak overnight from August 31 into September 1, normally producing only about 6 meteors per hour. But this shower has a history of rare, dramatic outbursts, briefly flaring to dozens of meteors an hour in years like 2007 and 2021. The debris comes from the long-period comet Kiess, which last visited the inner solar system over a century ago.

🌠 The catch this year is the Moon: a bright waning gibbous, over 80% lit, washing out fainter streaks. Block it behind a building, look toward Auriga rising in the northeast, and watch after midnight. The bright fireballs can still cut through.

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text: ALL EYES ON LABOR DAY WEEKEND FOR TROPICAL MOISTURE POTENTIAL IN SOCAL & SW🌀🌧️🌊confidence is increasing that tropical moisture will spread north toward California late this week and into the Labor Day Holiday Weekend, but there remains considerable uncertainty over how close the actual tropical system gets to Southern California. Invest 95E, currently a disorganized disturbance well south of Baja California, is expected to develop into Hurricane Marie later this week. The system should initially track northwest toward the waters off Baja California through Friday and Saturday. After that, the forecast becomes much more complicated. The large trough expected across the West Coast will play a major role in determining the eventual track. Ensemble guidance currently shows two primary scenarios: I] one turns the storm farther west and out to sea, II] while the other brings it farther north toward Southern California. Recent ensemble trends favor the farther-west solution, with only around a 5% chance of more direct or significant tropical cyclone impacts to Southern California. That does NOT mean California escapes impacts. Tropical moisture is looking increasingly likely to surge north. Some guidance brings moisture into the Southwest and California as early as Thursday night or Friday, with precipitation chances increasing further Friday through the weekend. Roughly 90% of GEFS and EPS ensemble members increase atmospheric moisture to very high levels across portions of the region by Friday and Saturday. The combination of that moisture and a Pacific trough near the West Coast could provide enough lift for showers and thunderstorms, potentially leading to areas of heavy rainfall. Exactly where and how much rain falls remains uncertain. Ensemble guidance suggests the extreme scenario remains relatively unlikely, with only around 5-10% of roughly 100 projections producing 2+ inches of rain in Southern California. Around 20-30% remain essentially dry, leaving some lighter rainfall as the more likely middle-ground scenario. There is also a low but non-zero chance of stronger easterly winds depending on the eventual track, which could create concerns for fire weather and downed trees. Confidence is higher in coastal impacts. Unless the storm makes a substantial turn westward after Saturday, a strong south swell could affect Southern California through Tuesday. Swells from Hurricane Karina may also still be present, while evening high tides approach 7+ feet by Labor Day Monday. That combination could produce high surf and moderate coastal flooding along south-facing beaches during the busy Labor Day weekend. A closer approach by the tropical system would amplify those impacts. The key message right now: a direct hit is unlikely, but an influx of tropical moisture and coastal impacts are becoming increasingly plausible. There are still plenty of moving pieces, especially since the tropical cyclone hasn't even formed yet. The forecast should become considerably clearer over the next 2-3 days once a defined circulation develops and models get a better handle on its interaction with the Western trough🌀🌧️🌊

items.text: TROPICAL STORM EDOUARD TRENDING STRONGER WITH RAIN THREAT EXPANDING INLAND🌀🌧️soon-to-be Tropical Storm Edouard is trending stronger, and that should allow its moisture and impacts to reach considerably farther inland across Texas and Oklahoma. The latest NHC forecast now brings the system to around 60 mph before landfall, followed by a northwestward track into East Texas. Rain chances are increasing farther north, with decent chances now extending toward the Red River and potentially even some showers reaching as far north as I-40 in Oklahoma. Across North Texas, the best opportunity for meaningful rainfall remains south and southeast of Dallas-Fort Worth. Parts of the southern DFW Metro could receive around 1 inch, although amounts will vary considerably depending on the exact track and organization of the system. Farther south, rainfall becomes much heavier. The Brazos Valley, Southeast Texas and Upper Texas Coast could see widespread 3-5 inches, with localized totals of 5-7 inches or more. The NHC is currently forecasting totals up to 9 inches for parts of the Upper Texas Coast, creating a significant flash-flood threat in the hardest-hit areas. The biggest change is that this is becoming less of a strictly coastal Southeast Texas rain event. A stronger and better-organized Edouard could transport deeper tropical moisture farther north before weakening, giving portions of Central and North Texas a better opportunity for some much-needed rainfall. There will still be a sharp rainfall gradient, so not everyone in North Texas or Oklahoma will see meaningful rain - rain will be confined to areas directly near the center of the system so small changes in Edouard's track and strength could drastically change which areas see heavy rain and which areas see no rain at all🌧️🌀

items.text: TROPICAL MOISTURE COULD BRING HEAVY RAIN TO THE WEST & SOUTHWEST🌧️🌀confidence continues to increase that a surge of tropical moisture from the Eastern Pacific could spread into a large part of the western United States during the first half of September. There is still considerable uncertainty regarding exactly where the deepest tropical moisture and heaviest rainfall ultimately track. Small changes in the track of the developing tropical system and the position of the western trough could dramatically change where the heaviest rain occurs. Still, this is becoming an important period to watch. A significant influx of tropical moisture could support multiple rounds of thunderstorms and locally heavy rainfall, particularly across the Southwest where flash flooding could become a concern. California and parts of the Great Basin could also receive unusually high moisture for early September. The signal is there but the details will become much clearer once the tropical system develops and models get a better handle on its eventual track🌀🌧️

items.text: STRONG EARLY-SEASON STORM TO HIT THE PACIFIC NORTHWEST THIS WEEK🌧️💨❄️a significant early-season storm will move into the Pacific Northwest Wednesday into Thursday, bringing widespread rain, gusty winds, much cooler temperatures and even a few thunderstorms. For the first days of September, this will be an unusually strong and fall-like system. Rain will become widespread across Washington and Oregon Wednesday into Thursday, reaching the Inland Northwest and portions of northern California. The coast could see 1-3 inches of rain, while the mountains and foothills could receive 2-4 inches below snow level. Snow levels will fall below 7,000 feet, and meaningful wetting rain is also expected east of the Cascades. This will be very beneficial for ongoing wildfires. While it probably won't completely end fire season, the combination of rain, cooler temperatures and higher humidity should significantly slow fire activity. Strong southerly winds will accompany the storm Wednesday. Gusts over 40 mph are possible along the Washington and Oregon coasts, Whidbey Island, San Juan Islands and western Whatcom County, with 25-35 mph gusts elsewhere. With trees still carrying full foliage and some stressed from the dry summer, isolated downed limbs and power outages are possible. Gale-force winds are also possible over coastal waters, with seas building to 8-12 feet. Temperatures will tumble to 15-20° below normal as colder air settles over the region. Isolated thunderstorms are also possible Wednesday and Thursday, capable of producing brief heavy rain, lightning, gusty winds and small hail. The first widespread rain after a long dry summer could make roads unusually slick, while isolated rockslides or debris flows are possible near steep terrain and recent burn scars in southern Oregon. Blowing dust is also possible across parts of the Columbia Basin and Okanogan Valley ahead of the rain Wednesday. Showers should linger into Friday and potentially parts of the weekend as the deep upper-level low remains over the Northwest, keeping the region cooler and unsettled🌧️💨❄️

items.text: TROPICAL RAIN SPREADS INTO TEXAS BUT HOW FAR NORTH WILL IT GET❓🌧️🌀Tropical Depression Five has formed in the northern Gulf and is expected to strengthen into Tropical Storm Edouard before making landfall along the Upper Texas Coast on Tuesday. While some tropical-storm-force winds are possible near the immediate coast, heavy rainfall and flash flooding will be the primary threats. The greatest concern is across Southeast Texas, where widespread rainfall totals of 3-5 inches are expected with isolated amounts of 6-9 inches, especially east of I-45. Tropical downpours could produce rainfall rates of 3-4 inches per hour at times, creating a risk of flash flooding Tuesday into early Wednesday. Farther inland, rainfall amounts become much more uncertain and generally lighter. Parts of South-Central Texas, particularly east of I-35 and closer to Highway 77, could see scattered showers and thunderstorms Tuesday and Wednesday. Most locations are expected to receive one-half inch or less, although isolated pockets of 1-2 inches will be possible. Across Central and North Texas, the remnants are expected to move northwestward near the I-45 corridor Tuesday night into Wednesday before weakening. Eastern portions of the region have the best opportunity for rain, with roughly 0.25-1 inch possible and isolated higher amounts. However, areas west of I-35 and north of I-20 may receive very little or no rain at all. The biggest question is Oklahoma. Some model guidance continues to bring the weakening remnants northward around the western edge of the heat dome, potentially allowing moisture, clouds and a few showers to reach portions of the state Wednesday through Friday. However, confidence in meaningful rainfall is LOW. The latest forecast only carries around a 20% chance of showers across parts of Southeast Oklahoma Thursday, while most of Oklahoma is currently expected to remain hot and dry. Because this is a small, compact tropical system, relatively minor changes in its track, organization and how quickly it weakens could make a major difference in how far inland the rain reaches❓🌧️🌀

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
NO HURRICANES YET: 2026 MOVING INTO RARE TERRITORY

It’s the last day of August, and we still haven’t had a hurricane form in the Atlantic. Not that anyone around here is complaining!

As of 2pm on August 31, 2026 ranks 8th for the latest first Atlantic hurricane of the satellite era, which began in 1966. And there’s a very good chance we’re not done climbing the list.

Tropical Storm Eduoard will form soon in the northern Gulf, but make landfall in Texas well below hurricane strength. So, it's a virtual lock that we won’t see a hurricane through Wednesday, which would move 2026 all the way into 5th place. More tropical waves will roll off the African coast over the next several weeks, but for now they’ll be fighting an uphill battle. Hostile wind shear and widespread sinking air, both characteristic of a very strong El Niño pattern, continue to dominate much of the tropical Atlantic. Those conditions make it extremely difficult for tropical systems to thrive.

Perhaps even more remarkable, none of our major forecast models currently develop a hurricane in the Atlantic during the next two weeks. If that forecast holds, 2026 could make a serious run at the record for the latest first hurricane of the modern satellite era: September 11, set by Gustav in 2002 and tied by Humberto in 2013.

There is an interesting historical footnote. The 1907 and 1914 seasons had no hurricanes in the official record, but both occurred long before satellites provided continuous coverage of the Atlantic. Back then, ships were one of the primary ways of discovering storms over the open ocean. A hurricane could form, spend its entire life at sea and dissipate without ever crossing a shipping route. And if ships knew a hurricane was nearby, they generally did their best to avoid it! So comparing those early seasons with today's satellite era isn't exactly apples to apples.

Keep in mind, we're just now entering the climatological peak of Atlantic hurricane season. A quiet start certainly doesn't mean we're in the clear. Mother Nature doesn't care about records or seasonal statistics, and it only takes one hurricane in the wrong place to turn an otherwise quiet season into a devastating one.

items.author: ryanhallyall
items.text: We've been watching Wednesday, September 2 for a few days now, and SPC just bumped it up to a Level 2 severe risk across Ohio, Pennsylvania, and New York. Damaging wind and large hail are the main concerns, and a tornado or two can't be ruled out. What's driving it: unusually cold air moving in a couple miles up will be riding over warm, humid air near the ground, which tends to make storms grow strong in a hurry. Forecasters think this could come in two separate rounds, one over the eastern Great Lakes in the afternoon and another moving through Pennsylvania and New York later in the day. Still two days out, so the exact line of storms will get some fine-tuning, but this is worth keeping on your radar.

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text: HURRICANE TROPICAL MARIE EXPECTED TO DEVELOP - TROPICAL MOISTURE COULD REACH CALIFORNIA & THE SOUTHWEST⚠️🌀🌧️a developing tropical system well offshore of southwestern Mexico is expected to become Hurricane Marie this week, and it could eventually play an important role in the weather across California and the Southwest during the upcoming Labor Day weekend. The disturbance, currently designated EP95, now has an 80% chance of developing within 48 hours and a 90% chance within seven days. A tropical depression is likely to form within the next couple of days as the system moves generally west-northwest to northwest. Once Marie develops, the system is expected to eventually gain more of a north-to-northwestward component. This could allow tropical moisture associated with the storm to become drawn northward toward California and parts of the Southwest heading into Labor Day weekend. There is increasing confidence that indirect impacts will occur, particularly an increase in tropical moisture that could lead to higher humidity, more clouds and increased opportunities for showers and thunderstorms across parts of the region. Depending on exactly how the pattern evolves, locally heavy rainfall could also become a concern. However, it remains too early to determine whether Marie itself will produce any direct impacts in California or the Southwest. There is still considerable spread among the forecast models regarding the eventual track and how close the system could get to the region. Forecast uncertainty remains high, especially since the system has not developed a well-defined center yet. Until a consolidated circulation forms, models are essentially trying to forecast the future track of a center that does not fully exist. Confidence should begin to increase once the main center forms and models have a better starting point. This will be an important system to watch closely through the week as Labor Day weekend approaches⚠️🌀🌧️

The National Hurricane Center could issue watches and warnings as soon as tonight or tomorrow morning. items.author: JeffBerardelli
items.text:
🌡️ 4-Factor FeelsLike Forecast 🌡️ 
It’s the feels-like in Sun and Wind!
The US heat this week will be extreme. 
Traditional heat index forecasts do NOT include the sun and wind. Odd right? I’ve always thought they should because some folks spend so much time exposed. So, I found a formula from Dr. Robert Steadman in a white paper, and it turns out one version is being used by the Australian Bureau of Meteorology right now. This 4-factor equation I’m using takes both into account. Sun spikes it. In sunny spots the sun adds ~ 15°! Generally wind cools it. For instance: Nashville in the shade is 105. Raleigh in the shade feels like 102. DC in the shade is 100. Atlanta in the shade is 97. Bottom line you can NOT directly compare this to our NOAA traditional heat index, and it should not be used to replace it. It does illustrate how being in the summer Sun makes a dramatic difference. So… shade is your friend this week. Be safe!!

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text: TROPICAL MOISTURE COULD SURGE INTO SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA NEXT WEEKEND🌴🌀🌧️ there are growing signals that tropical moisture could make a significant push northward into Southern California next weekend into early the following week, potentially bringing heavy rain, increased humidity, thunderstorms and strong south swells. A developing tropical disturbance off Mexico currently has a 90% chance of becoming a tropical cyclone within the next seven days. While it is far too early to know the eventual track or whether the tropical system itself gets anywhere near California, a notable number of ensemble and deterministic model solutions show the system - or a substantial plume of its moisture - being pulled northward from near Baja California toward Southern California. By next Sunday, the average precipitable water value among ensemble members climbs to around 1.5 inches, with several individual members exceeding 2 inches. Those would represent very high moisture levels for Southern California and could support periods of heavy rainfall if the necessary atmospheric lift develops. The evolving upper-level pattern will be critical. A cut-off low may linger near Northern California into the weekend, disrupting the typical subtropical ridge that often keeps tropical systems and their moisture confined farther south. If the trough remains near the West Coast, it could effectively open the door for tropical moisture to recurve northward toward California. There remains considerable uncertainty. Ensemble guidance still varies significantly regarding the position of the West Coast trough, the Southern Rockies ridge and the eventual tropical cyclone. Small changes in this pattern could mean the difference between deep tropical moisture reaching California or remaining largely offshore. For now, there is at least a chance of precipitation across Southern California next weekend, but confidence in exact rainfall amounts and locations remains low. This is not a forecast for a tropical cyclone landfall in California. The bigger concern at this stage is the possibility of a substantial tropical moisture surge producing heavy rain, thunderstorms, muggy tropical conditions and strong south swells. With roughly a week to go, expect plenty of changes in the forecast🌴🌀🌧️

All through late August, Venus has been creeping toward a distant blue-white star. Tonight, it arrives.

On September 1, Venus meets Spica in a close conjunction low in the west-southwest after sunset. The two make a striking odd couple: Venus, a planet just next door in cosmic terms, blazing as the Evening Star, and Spica, a searing binary star system some 250 light-years beyond it, its light having left before the telescope was even invented. Side by side, they look like near equals, yet Spica is millions of times farther away.

🔭 Because they hang low near the horizon, you'll want a clear western view and good timing, around 45 minutes after sunset. Both fit in a single binocular field. Catch them soon, as Spica will slip into the twilight in the nights that follow, while Venus climbs toward its greatest brilliance later this month ✨🌟
